premises.statement: Law is a rule and measure of acts.
Practical reason orders acts to an end, first among practical principles.
A principle is a measure and rule within its genus.
Universal practical propositions ordered to action have law character.
Law is in the regulator essentially and in regulated subjects participatively.
Rational operation is distinguished from its constituted product.
Practical universal propositions can be retained habitually.
Will directed to an end moves practical reason.
A ruler’s will has law character only insofar as reason regulates it.
The objection infers that law is not reason because law is named as being in bodily members.
The objection argues law is no power, habit, or act, and would cease during sleep.
The objection locates motion in will and cites the ruler’s pleasure.
The sed contra identifies commanding and forbidding with reason.

The source says law is a rule and measure and reason orders acts as a first principle; the inference that this makes law pertain to reason uses an explicit constitutive bridge from reason’s measuring role to the law’s rule-measure role. This bridge is assumed, not independently established.
